query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys exposed to a corrosive NaCl environment, sliding wear mechanically disrupts the self-healing passive oxide layer, exposing fresh metal that accelerates localized corrosion and, thereby, governs the overall tribo-corrosion degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeNi-based HEA) with an initially intact, self-healing passive oxide film formed in equilibrium with a NaCl-containing electrolyte.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled sliding wear (tribological motion) in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under identical NaCl immersion environments: one with static immersion to allow passive film stabilization, and one with repeated sliding wear to mechanically abrade the passive film. The tests should be run at room temperature and, if needed, compared across various sliding durations to observe cumulative effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity of the passive oxide film at the alloy surface, whose continuity protects the underlying metal from corrosive attack.
generation.mechanism: Sliding wear mechanically breaks down the passive oxide film, removing its protective barrier. This disruption allows for increased access of chloride ions to the fresh metal, promoting accelerated localized corrosion. The synergistic action of mechanical abrasion and electrochemical degradation leads to a higher total degradation than either wear or corrosion alone.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a static immersion baseline, the specimen subjected to combined sliding wear and corrosion will show (1) a higher overall degradation rate, (2) increased localized corrosion at the wear track (evidenced by lower impedance and visible pits), and (3) a larger wear volume. The coupled effect should be significantly greater than the sum of isolated wear and corrosion processes.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy specimen immersed in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution without any applied mechanical wear, where the passive film remains largely intact and corrosion proceeds at a slower, more uniform rate.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold for alloys and conditions in which a protective oxide layer forms readily and is susceptible to mechanical disruption. It may fail or be significantly altered in cases where the alloy exhibits an exceptionally robust passive film (with rapid re-passivation) or if operating conditions (e.g., extremely high temperatures or altered pH) change the film formation/repair dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of degradation acceleration (i.e., the exact magnitude of increased corrosion rate or wear volume) is uncertain without specific experimental data, and interactions may vary with alloy composition and environmental parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy specimens with verified passive oxide films. Subject one set to static immersion in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution and the other to identical immersion combined with controlled sliding wear using a tribometer. Monitor the surface condition at predetermined time intervals using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), potentiodynamic polarization, and surface microscopy (e.g., SEM) combined with XPS to assess the integrity of the oxide film and extent of localized corrosion.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance (to assess passive film resistance)
Potentiodynamic polarization curves (to determine corrosion rates)
Wear scar analysis (optical or SEM imaging and profilometry)
XPS analysis for oxide film chemistry and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sliding wear specimen does not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in passive film integrity (evidenced by no significant change in EIS or XPS results) or if its overall degradation rate (both wear and corrosion) is similar to or lower than that of the static immersion specimen, then the hypothesis that mechanical disruption of the passive film governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response would be falsified.

For each concentration, no obvious corrosion pit was observed on the whole surface. This result is consistent with the XPS findings that the corrosion resistance of the C1 RHEA in 13.5 wt% or 23.5wt% NaCl solution was as good as that in 3.5 wt%. In addition, the integrity of the surface also confirmed the reliability of the XPS results. These results provide additional evidence for the excellent corrosion resistance of the Nb25Mo25Ta25Ti20W5Cx RHEAs in high-concentration NaCl solutions. Combined with the corroded morphology shown in Figure 2e,f, the microstructure of these RHEAs showed no obvious changes after corrosion. Further understandings of the effect of microstructural change may also be helpful for elucidating the underlying corrosive mechanisms of these alloys in future. Moreover, for practical applications in harsh corrosive environments, including marine engineering and power plants, other factors such as pH may also affect the corrosion resistance of the RHEAs significantly.
